The authors derive two equations of state that link the eigenvalues of the permittivity and permeability tensors to the geometric transformation, allowing for broadband cloaking.
The example cloak design uses a plasma-like dispersive behavior for the radial components of permittivity and permeability, with the orthogonal components calculated using the derived equations.

The maximum theoretical bandwidth of the cloak is contained within the interval [ω_min, ω_0], where ω_min is the plasma frequency at the external boundary and ω_0 is the maximum frequency of operation.
As the frequency decreases, the number of layers contributing to the cloaking effect is reduced, leading to a decrease in the attenuation of the radar cross section.
The authors note that the exotic dispersion profile required for the orthogonal permittivity and permeability components may be challenging to realize in practice.

The proposed cloak design differs from previous work by directly linking the frequency-dependent material properties to the geometric transformation, allowing for broadband cloaking without compromising performance.
Transformation optics is the key concept behind the cloak design, allowing the authors to mimic a distorted virtual electromagnetic space using a special distribution of matter.
The authors show that the frequency-dispersive material properties do not disrupt the cloaking as long as the derived equations of state are satisfied, even with extreme anisotropy and inhomogeneity.

The ability to design broadband cloaking devices using dispersive metamaterials could enable a wide range of applications, such as electromagnetic shielding, stealth technology, and the control of wave propagation in complex environments.
The authors perform full-wave simulations to validate the theory, demonstrating the frequency-dependent cloaking effect and the attenuation of the radar cross section.
The authors note that their analysis neglects losses, which would need to be considered for a more realistic design of the frequency-dispersive cloak.
The proposed cloak design uses a multilayered structure, with each layer composed of an anisotropic theoretical material with frequency-dependent permittivity and permeability tensors.
The authors derive a constitutive relation between the radial and orthogonal components of the permittivity and permeability tensors, ensuring the required optical path for cloaking.
The authors establish two equivalent systems of equations that describe the conditions for achieving broadband cloaking with frequency-dispersive materials.

The authors suggest that the exotic dispersion profile required for the orthogonal permittivity and permeability components could potentially be approximated using a combination of high-pass or band-pass filters and regular dielectrics.
